title: Private deployments: VPC & On-Prem combined deployment, Day-2 ops, upgrade and rollback, and customer requirements library
author: Aisha Kapoor
body:
Overview

This document is a consolidated reference for Redwood Inference private deployments: VPC-hosted and on-prem packaging. It combines deployment guidance (network and infra), reference architectures, packaging requirements for on-prem installations, Day-2 operational procedures, and a prescriptive upgrade + rollback playbook. Target audience: SREs, platform engineers, and customer success teams supporting enterprise private deployments.

Scope and intent

- Provide a single, tested runbook for initial deployment, verification, and Day-2 operations.
- Capture minimum customer requirements (networking, security, capacity, compliance) required to start a deployment engagement.
- Describe upgrade and rollback procedures (canary -> progressive -> full) and clearly defined rollback triggers.
- Define ownership, SLOs, and monitoring expectations for Private deployments.

Prerequisites and assumptions

- Customer has approved network design and provided required VPC peering, firewall rules, and KMS/HSM integration details.
- For on-prem: target cluster meets hardware/OS packaging requirements (see Packaging Requirements table below).
- SSH and admin-level access to customer bastion/jump host for deployment tasks.
- Access to Redwood private repo for install artifacts and signed packages.

Audience and ownership

- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team.
- Day-to-day ops owner after handoff: customer (with Redwood SRE on-call during warranty) or Redwood Dedicated support when specified in contract.
- Escalation: follow customer success escalation playbook (see related_pages).

Reference architectures (high level)

1) VPC-hosted private deployment (recommended for cloud-first customers)

- Components: Control plane (Redwood-managed or customer-hosted control plane), Data plane (model-serving nodes in private VPC), Load balancers (internal), Bastion/jump host, optional NAT/Gateway for egress.
- Availability: Recommend 3 AZs for model-serving and control-plane proxies; cross-AZ LB.
- Networking: Private subnets for serving nodes, restricted management subnet for control plane, explicit peering/VPN to customer network.
- Security: Private subnets with no public IPs on serving nodes; KMS integration for encryption-at-rest. RBAC via SSO/OIDC for console and API.

Diagram (textual):
- customer-vpc (private) -> transit-gateway -> redwood-managed-control-plane (if customer opts for hosted control plane)
- model-servers in private subnets (GKE/AKS/EKS or self-managed k8s) -> internal NLB -> customer app network

2) On-prem packaged deployment (recommended for air-gapped/regulatory customers)

- Components: On-prem appliance (VM or bare-metal nodes), container runtime (containerd), Kubernetes distribution (RKE2/AKS-D/OE-supported), private registry, optional offline KMS/HSM.
- Packaging: Secure tarball or OCI bundle with signed artifacts + installer CLI. Installer supports offline verification and package checksum verification.

On-prem packaging requirements (minimum)

Area | Minimum requirement | Notes
---|---:|---
CPUs | 32 vCPU per model node (x86_64, AVX2+) | Baseline for small-medium deployments
GPU | 4x A100 80GB or equivalent per serving pool | Depends on model/throughput requirements
Memory | 512 GB RAM per GPU node | KV cache & batching needs
Disk | 2TB NVMe for local cache + 10TB backup storage | Ensure write performance for caching
OS | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (kernel >=5.15) or RHEL 8.6 | SELinux permissive during install recommended
Network | 10 Gbps interconnect, MTU 9000 recommended | Low intra-cluster latency critical
KMS/HSM | Customer KMS with PKCS#11 or AWS KMS endpoint via proxy | Keys must be available before install

Note: sizing varies by model family and target latency/throughput — reference the capacity planning worksheet in related_pages.

Customer requirements library (quick checklist)

Network
- Private subnets for serving nodes with CIDR ranges provided.
- Internal load balancers allowed between subnets.
- Specific firewall rules (examples):
  - Allow TCP 22 from Redwood jump host CIDR for install windows.
  - Allow TCP 443/8443 from app networks to internal LB.
  - Allow outbound to KMS endpoints (if customer-managed KMS).

Security & Compliance
- Identity: OIDC provider or SAML SSO configured for admin console access.
- Audit logging: Centralized syslog collector or SIEM integration required.
- Data residency: Confirm storage encryption and retention policy.
- Background checks: Hostlist for any resumed Redwood engineers requiring on-site access.

Operational
- NTP sync sources provided.
- Backup target (S3-compatible endpoint) with credentials for scheduled backups.
- Monitoring endpoints (Prometheus pushgateway or pull) reachable by Redwood observability collector.

Capacity & Performance
- Target peak RPS and average sequence length.
- Expected p95 and p99 latency targets for inference.
- Spike/burst requirements (burst allowance in contract).

Deployment procedure (high level)

1) Pre-deployment validation (run by Redwood Solutions Engineer)
- Verify customer prerequisites from checklist.
- Obtain access windows and change control approvals.
- Validate KMS integration and certificate chains.
- Confirm on-prem hardware firmware and BIOS settings (power management disabled).

2) Installer preparation
- For VPC: Ensure IAM roles, service account creation, and private repo access tokens are ready.
- For on-prem: Transfer signed bundle and verify sha256 checksums.

3) Initial install (example commands)

# Download installer (example, VPC)
curl -o redwood-installer.sh https://private.repo.redwood/internal/installer/latest
chmod +x redwood-installer.sh
./redwood-installer.sh --mode=vpc --control-plane-endpoint https://cp.example.internal --k8s-context mycluster

# On-prem offline install (example)
scp redwood-bundle.tar.gz installer@bastion:/tmp/
ssh installer@bastion 'sha256sum /tmp/redwood-bundle.tar.gz'
ssh installer@bastion 'sudo ./redwood-install --offline --bundle /tmp/redwood-bundle.tar.gz --install-dir /opt/redwood'

4) Post-install verification (smoke tests)
- Verify all pods are in Ready state: kubectl get pods -n redwood-system --no-headers | grep -v Running
- Run inference smoke test against internal endpoint: curl -s -X POST https://internal-lb/v1/generate -d '{"input":"test"}' | jq .
- KV cache warm-up: run 10 short synthetic requests and verify cache hit ratio > 30% after warmup.

Day-2 operations (runbook)

Monitoring & alerting
- Required metrics: token-per-second, request-latency-p95, GPU-utilization, KV-cache-hit-rate, model-load-errors.
- Alerts (examples):
  - token-per-second drops > 50% sustained for 10m -> P2
  - request-latency-p95 > latency_target*1.5 for 5m -> P1
  - GPU memory OOM events -> P0 (pager)

Regular tasks
1) Daily
- Check health dashboard (console) and reconcile any failing checks.
- Verify backups completed successfully.

2) Weekly
- Rotate short-lived API keys and verify service-to-service tokens.
- Review anomaly/quality alerts from Redwood Optimize.

3) Monthly
- Capacity review and anticipated model changes.
- Security patch maintenance window planning.

Backups and disaster recovery
- Configuration backups: store k8s manifests and Helm values in git (encrypted repo).
- Daily snapshot of local cache metadata and model pointers to long-term storage.
- Restore validation: perform a quarterly test restore in a staging environment.

Upgrade strategy and playbook

Principles
- Upgrades are performed as: canary -> progressive -> full.
- Each phase has automated health checks and rollback criteria.
- All upgrades must start in staging and pass a predefined test battery before reaching production.

Pre-upgrade checklist
- Validate backups and snapshot completion.
- Notify customers and stake holders per SLA (at least 72h before major upgrades).
- Ensure canary subset of serving nodes has <5% of traffic and health checks passing.

Canary upgrade steps (example)
1) Deploy new version to canary pool (5% traffic).
2) Run smoke test suite and quality evals (prompt sets).
3) Monitor health metrics for 30m (latency, errors, GPU mem).
4) If metrics stable, promote to progressive.

Progressive & full rollout
- Progressive: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 30-60m observation windows between steps.
- Full: redeploy remaining nodes once stable at 50%.

Rollback criteria (triggers)
- p95 latency increases > 30% vs pre-upgrade baseline for 10m.
- Error rate (5xx) increases > 2x baseline for 5m.
- Model quality regression detected by Redwood Optimize (fail any critical prompt set).

Rollback procedure (fast path)
1) Isolate failing pool and shift traffic to previous stable pool using routing controls.
2) Revert deployment in k8s via helm rollback or image rollback: helm rollback redwood-serving 2
3) Confirm smoke tests pass and latencies return to baseline.
4) Open postmortem and tag the release pipeline with failure metadata.

Detailed rollback (if fast path fails)
- Execute full cluster rollback using stored manifests (restore from git commit tagged as last-known-good).
- Restore model pointers and KV cache metadata from snapshots.

Testing and validation

Automated test suite (required)
- Smoke tests (connectivity, simple generation).
- Load tests at 10% and 50% of expected peak.
- Quality evals using curated prompt sets; evaluate p50/p95 coherence and hallucination checks.

Manual validation
- Engage customer product/ML owners to run 10-20 representative prompt sets before major releases.

Troubleshooting common failure modes

1) Slow inference after upgrade
- Check GPU utilization and CPU steal (top + nvidia-smi).
- Inspect kernel selection logs (redwood-runtime logs) for fallback to slower kernels.
- Re-run warm-up workload and verify KV cache hit-rate.

2) Deployment pods CrashLoopBackOff
- kubectl describe pod and review events.
- Check configmaps and secret mounts; verify checksum of config artifact.

3) KMS failures
- Validate network reachability to KMS endpoint and TLS cert chain.
- Review key rotation logs and ensure key versions match installer manifest.

Runbook: escalation and postmortem

- P0 incidents: page on-call SRE and execute incident bridge.
- P1/P2 incidents: resolve within 4-24 hours per SLA; track in incident tracker.
- Postmortem: owner writes postmortem within 72 hours; include timeline, impact, root cause, corrective actions, and follow-ups (owner + due dates).

Operational metrics and SLOs (recommended defaults)
- Uptime SLO: 99.9% monthly for serving endpoints (customer may request stricter SLA in contract).
- Latency SLO: p95 < configured target (document configured per deployment).
- Error budget and alerting thresholds included in SLO document referenced in related_pages.

Appendix A: Example Helm values (snippet)

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  internalPort: 8443
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "8"
    memory: "32Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: "32"
    memory: "256Gi"
models:
  default:
    replicas: 2
    modelName: "redwood-llama-3b"

Appendix B: Change control and approval matrix

- Minor change (non-breaking config changes): Redwood change window (24-72h notice).
- Major change (model upgrades, kernel/runtime changes): 72h notice, at least one customer sign-off.

Appendix C: Contacts and ownership

- Eng-private-deployments owner: aisha.kapoor@redwood.ai
- SRE on-call: sre-oncall@redwood.ai (pager duty)
- Customer success: assigned per account (see sales-enablement docs).
